clue.text: Beastly sort in river

blocks.note: surface reading: some nasty character found in a river
setter's reading: an animal whose Greek name means 'river horse'

explanation.surface: A villainous type lurking in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' suggests nastiness, but it just means an actual beast; hippopotamus is Greek for river horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The short form of hippopotamus names a large African animal that lives largely in rivers and lakes.

clue.text: Book aggressive player

blocks.note: first meaning: a book bound in stiff covers
second meaning: a tough, uncompromising defender in football or rugby

explanation.surface: Booking a rough player, as a referee would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like the referee's verb, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a stiff-covered volume and a tough defender who tackles hard in a team sport.

clue.text: Going round in circles, with constant polling?

blocks.note: pi is the mathematical constant
polling is casting votes

explanation.surface: Endless opinion polls leave everyone going round in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: Pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, neatly echoes the circles of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pivoting is turning about a fixed point, so rotating round and round in a circle.

clue.text: Prepare to bait line perhaps, and give oneself problems

blocks.note: first meaning, literal: an angler unseals a tin of bait
second meaning, idiomatic: stir up a mass of complications

explanation.walkthrough: The literal angling sense and the idiom are the same words; 'perhaps' flags that baiting a line is only one reason.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means starting something that unleashes many unforeseen difficulties, while literally a fisherman gets out bait.

clue.text: Poor lad is hit: beginning of painful shiner

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so the letters that follow are knocked into a new order
the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
to lam is to thrash or hit
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A poor boy has been punched, and a painful black eye is starting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shiner' looks like the black eye of the surface, but it means anything that shines. An Aldis lamp is a signalling lamp used at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A shiner is something that gives out light, and an Aldis lamp is a hand-held signalling light flashing Morse code.

clue.text: Word of approval detailing change

indicators.note: de-tailing means taking the tail off, so the last letter of the following word goes

blocks.note: to amend is to change

explanation.surface: Someone says yes to a detailed alteration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailing' reads as itemising, but split it as de-tailing: removing the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Amen is said after a prayer to signal agreement, meaning 'so be it', a word of assent.

clue.text: Throw party at noon? A sure-fire winner!

blocks.note: a disco is a dance party
N for noon
a cert is a certainty, a horse sure to win

explanation.surface: Holding a party at midday is guaranteed to succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw' looks like throwing a party, but it is the definition: to throw someone is to fluster them. Cert is British betting slang.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw a person is to confuse or unsettle them, which is what disconcert means.

clue.text: In Victoria, perhaps, an Australian native gets very warm reception

indicators.note: in means what follows sits inside the place Victoria exemplifies

blocks.note: Victoria is a London railway station; 'perhaps' marks it as one example
taken as written
the dingo is Australia's wild dog
V for very

explanation.surface: In the Australian state of Victoria, a local is greeted very warmly.
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria looks like the Australian state, matching the surface, but it is the London terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: A standing ovation is an audience rising to applaud, an especially enthusiastic and warm welcome.

clue.text: Give out an indication one has heard

indicators.note: what one has heard is the spoken sound, not the spelling

blocks.note: a sign is an indication

explanation.surface: Someone signals that they have caught what was said.
explanation.definitionFit: To assign tasks is to allot or allocate them, handing them out among people.

clue.text: Youngster’s favourite entertainer

blocks.note: pop, as in a pop star, a popular entertainer
a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A child's best-loved performer.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the reverse of clue order. Poppet is a British term of endearment for a small child.
explanation.definitionFit: Poppet is an affectionate name for a small child, a darling youngster.

clue.text: Could they be awfully severe with writer? Not half!

definitions.text: Could they be awfully severe with writer? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means only half of the preceding word survives, the rest being dropped
done awfully means done badly, so the letters are jumbled out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut to its first half

explanation.surface: Critics might savage an author, the clue suggests, with a cheeky 'not half' of agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' reads as British slang for 'very much so', but it trims the last word to its first three letters. The whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Reviewers are critics who write assessments of books, and they can indeed be harsh towards an author.

clue.text: Article taking stance about author

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the word for stance is read back to front

blocks.note: the indefinite article
a pose is a posture or stance

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece takes a position on some writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop is the ancient Greek storyteller credited with the famous collection of animal fables.

clue.text: Lay with fellow on grass

blocks.note: to lay money is to bet it
Ray, a man's name, standing for any fellow

explanation.surface: Lying down on the lawn with a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' looks like the lawn, but it is the slang verb meaning to inform on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To grass is British slang for informing to the police, a way of betraying a confederate.

clue.text: French region visited about end of summer with loyal friend

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, which alone is kept
about means surrounding, so the word for visited wraps round what follows

blocks.note: having done a place is having visited it as a tourist
its closing letter
the dog is proverbially man's most loyal friend

explanation.surface: A holiday in a part of France late in summer, taking the dog along.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'do' a place is tourist slang for visiting it, so DONE goes round the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dordogne is a department and river valley in south-west France, popular with British holidaymakers.

clue.text: In play, interval too short for a breather

indicators.note: letters in play are moved about freely, ending in a fresh order
too short means one letter is lacking, so the phrase loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written, then trimmed by one letter

explanation.surface: At a theatre, the interval is too brief for anyone to catch their breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A breather' poses as a rest, but it is something that breathes for a patient.
explanation.definitionFit: A ventilator is a machine that breathes for a patient, so it is literally a breather.

clue.text: One’s getting better drinks served cold in sister’s place

indicators.note: drinks served in a place are placed inside it, so they go within the sister's home

blocks.note: a convent is where nuns, or sisters, live
ales are beers
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A patient recovers with cold beers served at a nunnery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's getting better' is a whole-phrase definition for a person recovering, not a comparison.
explanation.definitionFit: A convalescent is a person recovering health after an illness, someone on the mend.

clue.text: Social worker with word of advice about drink

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word of advice goes round the drink

blocks.note: W is short for with
a hint is a word of advice
tea, the drink

explanation.surface: A social worker offers some advice over a cup of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' is not a welfare officer but a worker caste insect living in a colony. Here 'with' is a letter, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The white ant, or termite, is a social insect, and workers form the labouring caste of its colony.

clue.text: One of the Brontés healthy after high fibre food

indicators.note: after says the word for healthy is placed second, behind the food word

blocks.note: bran is the fibrous husk of cereal
well means healthy

explanation.surface: A Brontë sister in good health after a high-fibre diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the healthy word second. Branwell was the brother of Charlotte, Emily and Anne.
explanation.definitionFit: Branwell Brontë was the painter brother of the three novelist sisters, so one of that family.

clue.text: Fine and so laid back, having session with different carer

indicators.note: laid back here means put down backwards, so the little word so is read in reverse

blocks.note: F for fine, as on pencil leads
taken as written
a term is a session at school or in court
other means different

explanation.surface: A relaxed, cheerful person has a meeting with a new carer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid back' poses as relaxed, but it turns the short word backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A foster mother is a woman who looks after a child not her own, a carer in that sense.

clue.text: Ultimately generous deed: fellow’s carried bag

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the last letter is kept
the deed has carried the fellow, holding him inside it

blocks.note: its closing letter
an act is a deed
he, any male fellow; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: A kind act at last: a man carried someone's bag for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow's carried' means the fellow has been carried, by the deed.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachet is a small sealed bag or packet, holding something like sugar or shampoo.

clue.text: Game of cards cut short after ace goes missing

indicators.note: whatever goes missing is removed, so the letter for ace disappears

blocks.note: to abridge is to shorten
A for ace, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: A card game is curtailed once the ace is lost.
explanation.walkthrough: The ace of the surface seems part of the card game, but it is just the letter to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridge is the trick-taking card game for four players in two partnerships.

clue.text: Seeing wild animal, drivers move steadily backwards on road

indicators.note: backwards says the word for moving steadily is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: the Automobile Association, the British motoring organisation for drivers
RD is the abbreviation for road
to flow is to move along steadily

explanation.surface: Motorists spot a wild animal and slowly reverse along the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The AA is the Automobile Association, Britain's big motoring club, whose members are drivers. 'Seeing' just links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The aardwolf is a hyena-like mammal of southern and eastern Africa that feeds mainly on termites.

clue.text: Presumably lass repulsed English scientist

indicators.note: repulsed means driven back, so the letters are turned round

blocks.note: a lass is presumably not a lad

explanation.surface: A girl rejected some English scientist's advances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Presumably' signals a playful inference: a lass is, one assumes, 'not lad'. John Dalton developed atomic theory.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dalton was the English chemist and physicist who pioneered modern atomic theory and studied colour blindness.

clue.text: Man’s name entered in order form the wrong way

indicators.note: something entered in a phrase sits within it, spanning its words
the wrong way means back to front, so the letters run from right to left

blocks.note: letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A man's name filled in backwards on an order form.
explanation.walkthrough: The name runs from the F of 'form' back into the end of 'order'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fred is a common male first name, short for Frederick, so a man's name.

clue.text: Concealer right for putting on skin

blocks.note: a hide is an animal's skin
R for right

explanation.surface: A make-up concealer that is just right to put on your skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealer' suggests cosmetics but simply means one who hides.
explanation.definitionFit: A hider is someone or something that conceals, so the two nouns name the same doer.

clue.text: Stop unpleasant characters barring entrance in art gallery

indicators.note: barring the entrance shuts out the first letter, so the word loses its head
in places the shortened word inside the gallery's name

blocks.note: the Tate, the London art galleries
vermin are nasty, obnoxious people

explanation.surface: Halt undesirables who are blocked from getting into a gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the group of national art galleries in London and elsewhere in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To terminate something is to bring it to an end, which is the verb sense of halt.

clue.text: Not even Tories like classy wine that’s extremely dear

indicators.note: not even means the letters in odd positions only, skipping every second one

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
as means like
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U
red wine

explanation.surface: Conservatives are said to be fond of posh wine that costs a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from the 1950s British debate on 'U and non-U' usage. 'Extremely dear' looks like a price but means much loved.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured is greatly loved and valued, so it is very dear to its owner.

clue.text: In former province, native forsakes ancient city

indicators.note: forsakes means abandons, so the ancient city leaves the longer word

blocks.note: native talent is natural talent
Ur, the ancient Sumerian city

explanation.surface: In some old province, a local leaves a city of antiquity.
explanation.walkthrough: Ur of the Chaldees is the crossword's favourite ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, when it became KwaZulu-Natal.
